alternative: Carry the payload as a constructor parameter of the class, or of an intermediate class that holds the early-initialised value and extends the base (abstract class StreamInit(val buf: Buffer) extends Stream(buf)); Scala 3 trait parameters do the same job where a trait owns the value. For private subclass state that superclass code touches, move it into a nested object that is initialised on demand. Early initializers, the construct that did this, are dropped in Scala 3.
idiom_name: none - early initializers are dropped; the payload must be a constructor or trait parameter
implementation_notes: Scala 2 had exactly one construct for this problem - the early initializer (class C extends { val buf = ... } with Stream(buf)) - and the Scala 3 migration guide records it as deprecated in 2.13 and dropped in Scala 3, with the compiler error 'Early definitions are not supported; use trait parameters instead'. The documented replacements are the ones to use here: trait parameters (passed at the mixing site), an intermediate class that carries the early-initialised vals as constructor parameters, or a secondary constructor with a fixed value; for private subclass state read through an overridden method, a nested object that is initialised on demand. Constructor parameters are evaluated before the superclass body runs, so the payload must arrive as a parameter rather than as a val the superclass constructor could read - a trait's abstract val is not available to the superclass constructor either.
pitfalls: An abstract or overridden val read from the superclass constructor still sees null in Scala 3 - the hazard early initializers were used to work around - and the compiler cannot detect it, so the failure appears at runtime as a NullPointerException or a wrong value.
Trait parameters are not cross-compilable with Scala 2.13 and are supplied at the mixing site, so a library that must build under both versions needs the intermediate-class form instead.

The nested-object fix for superclass code that reads subclass state changes the identity model: the state lives in a singleton inside the instance rather than in the instance itself, which is fine for a mutable counter but wrong when the value must be per-instance observable.
